title: Sound
tagline: Study reflection of sound, echo, resonance and characteristics of sound waves.

overview.intro: Sound is a mechanical wave produced by vibrating objects and transmitted through a medium. This chapter examines reflection of sound, echo and its applications, conditions for hearing distinct echoes, resonance and natural frequency, and characteristics of sound such as loudness, pitch and quality. Numerical problems involving speed of sound and echo distances are also included.

learningOutcomes: Describe reflection of sound and conditions for formation of echo and reverberation.
Solve numerical problems involving echo, speed, distance and time.
Explain free vibrations, forced vibrations and resonance with examples.
Relate loudness, pitch and quality to amplitude, frequency and waveform.
Identify applications of echo and resonance in practical situations.

blocks.text: Sound waves reflect from surfaces following laws similar to light: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident wave, reflected wave and normal lie in the same plane. Hard surfaces such as walls, cliffs and buildings reflect sound well, while soft materials absorb it.

An echo is the repetition of sound heard after reflection from a distant surface. To hear a distinct echo, the reflected sound must reach the ear at least about 0.1 s after the original sound due to persistence of hearing. At a speed of about 340 m/s in air, this requires the reflecting surface to be at least about 17 m away (total distance travelled ~34 m).

items.text: Clapping near a distant wall and hearing the sound again.
items.note: The reflected sound is the echo.

items.text: Total distance = 2d, so d = vt/2 for echo problems.
items.note: Sound travels to the reflector and back.

blocks.text: Reverberation is the persistence of sound in an enclosed space due to repeated reflections from walls, ceiling and other surfaces. Excessive reverberation makes speech unclear in halls, so auditoriums use sound-absorbing materials such as curtains, carpets and acoustic panels to reduce it.

Echoes are used in applications such as SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) to measure depth of seas and locate underwater objects, in medical ultrasonography to image internal organs, and in determining distances or detecting obstacles. These methods rely on measuring the time taken for reflected sound or ultrasound to return.

items: Distinct echo requires sufficient time gap and distance.
Reverberation is due to multiple reflections in enclosed spaces.
SONAR uses ultrasonic waves in water for ranging and detection.

learn.title: Free Vibrations, Forced Vibrations and Resonance

blocks.text: When a body vibrates with its own natural frequency without external periodic force after being disturbed, it undergoes free (natural) vibrations, such as a tuning fork struck gently. When a body is made to vibrate by an external periodic force, it undergoes forced vibrations, and its frequency becomes that of the applied force.

Resonance occurs when the frequency of the applied force equals the natural frequency of a body, causing it to vibrate with maximum amplitude. Examples include a tuning fork causing another identical fork to sound loudly, and air columns resonating in musical instruments. Resonance can be useful but may also be destructive if amplitudes become excessive.

items.meaning: Frequency at which a body vibrates freely when disturbed.
Phenomenon of large-amplitude vibration when driving frequency equals natural frequency.
Persistence of sound due to repeated reflections in an enclosure.

blocks.text: Sounds are characterised by loudness, pitch and quality (timbre). Loudness is the sensation related to the amplitude of vibration; greater amplitude produces a louder sound. It is also influenced by distance from source and area of the vibrating body. Pitch is related to frequency: higher frequency sounds have higher pitch.

Quality or timbre enables us to distinguish between sounds of the same loudness and pitch produced by different sources, such as different musical instruments or voices. It depends on the waveform, which is determined by the fundamental frequency and overtones present in the sound.

The relation between speed (v), frequency (f) and wavelength (λ) of a wave is v = fλ. For sound, speed depends on the medium and its conditions, while frequency is determined by the source. In echo problems, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the total distance is twice the distance between source and reflector.

When solving numericals, convert units consistently and identify whether the given time corresponds to one-way or two-way travel. For multiple echoes or time intervals, interpret the situation carefully. Clear steps and correct formula selection are important for accurate answers.

items: Use d = vt/2 for simple echo distance calculations.
Persistence of hearing is about 0.1 s for distinct echo condition.
Pitch increases with frequency; loudness increases with amplitude.
Resonance gives maximum amplitude at natural frequency.

Echo is heard when reflected sound reaches after about 0.1 s; minimum distance in air is about 17 m.
In echo problems, sound travels to and fro, so distance = vt/2.
Reverberation is persistence of sound due to repeated reflections in enclosed spaces.
Resonance occurs when driving frequency equals natural frequency, producing large amplitude.
Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency and quality on waveform.

SONAR and ultrasonography use reflected sound/ultrasound for detection and imaging.
Hard surfaces reflect sound well; soft materials absorb sound.
Correct time and distance interpretation is essential in numerical problems.

questions.prompt: Sound cannot travel through:
questions.answer: vacuum
questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium for propagation.
questions.commonMistake: Light can travel through vacuum, but sound cannot.

questions.prompt: The persistence of hearing in humans is about:
questions.explanation: A reflected sound must reach at least about 0.1 s later to be heard as a distinct echo.
questions.commonMistake: This value determines the minimum distance for a distinct echo.

questions.prompt: Pitch of a sound depends on its:
questions.answer: frequency
questions.explanation: Higher frequency corresponds to higher pitch (shriller sound).
questions.commonMistake: Loudness depends on amplitude, not pitch.

questions.prompt: Resonance occurs when:
options: frequency of applied force equals natural frequency
questions.answer: frequency of applied force equals natural frequency
questions.explanation: At resonance, the body vibrates with maximum amplitude.
questions.commonMistake: Resonance is a frequency-matching condition.

questions.prompt: If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, the minimum distance of a reflecting surface for a distinct echo is about:
questions.explanation: Total distance = v × t = 340 × 0.1 = 34 m, so one-way distance = 17 m.
questions.commonMistake: Divide by 2 because sound travels to the reflector and back.

questions.prompt: Loudness of sound is related to:
questions.answer: amplitude
questions.explanation: Greater amplitude of vibration produces a louder sound.
questions.commonMistake: Pitch and quality depend on different factors.

questions.prompt: The relation between speed, frequency and wavelength of sound is:
questions.answer: v = fλ
questions.explanation: Wave speed equals the product of frequency and wavelength.
questions.commonMistake: Keep the variables in the correct positions.

questions.prompt: Quality (timbre) of a sound helps to distinguish:
options: loud and soft sounds of same source
sounds of same loudness and pitch from different sources
questions.answer: sounds of same loudness and pitch from different sources
questions.explanation: Quality depends on waveform/overtones and identifies the source of sound.
questions.commonMistake: Loudness and pitch are different characteristics from quality.

questions.prompt: The repetition of sound caused by reflection is called an ________.
questions.answer: echo
questions.explanation: An echo is heard when reflected sound returns after a sufficient time interval.
questions.commonMistake: Reverberation involves multiple reflections and persistence of sound.

questions.prompt: When driving frequency equals natural frequency, the phenomenon observed is ________.
questions.answer: resonance
questions.explanation: Resonance results in vibrations of maximum amplitude.
questions.commonMistake: Forced vibration alone does not necessarily produce resonance.

questions.prompt: The shrillness of a sound is determined by its ________.
questions.answer: frequency
questions.explanation: Higher frequency sounds are perceived as more shrill (higher pitch).
questions.commonMistake: Amplitude affects loudness, not shrillness.

questions.prompt: What is an echo?
questions.answer: An echo is the sound heard after reflection from a distant surface, arriving after the original sound with a sufficient time gap to be heard distinctly.
questions.explanation: Reflection and persistence of hearing together make an echo distinguishable.
questions.commonMistake: Mention reflection from a distant surface.

questions.prompt: State the condition for hearing a distinct echo in air.
questions.answer: The reflected sound must reach the listener at least 0.1 s after the original sound. At about 340 m/s in air, the reflecting surface must be at least about 17 m away.
questions.explanation: This ensures the echo is heard separately due to persistence of hearing.
questions.commonMistake: Give the minimum distance or time condition clearly.

questions.prompt: A person hears an echo 0.5 s after clapping. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, calculate the distance of the reflecting surface.
questions.answer: Total distance travelled by sound = v × t = 340 × 0.5 = 170 m. Distance of reflecting surface = total distance/2 = 170/2 = 85 m.
questions.explanation: Sound travels to the surface and returns, so the one-way distance is half the total.
questions.commonMistake: Do not forget to divide by 2 for echo problems.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between loudness and pitch of sound.
questions.answer: Loudness is the sensation that determines how loud or soft a sound is and depends mainly on the amplitude of vibration. Pitch is the sensation that determines how shrill or flat a sound is and depends on the frequency of vibration. Thus, loudness relates to amplitude while pitch relates to frequency.
questions.explanation: Each characteristic depends on a different physical property of the wave.
questions.commonMistake: Do not interchange amplitude and frequency.

questions.prompt: Explain free vibrations, forced vibrations and resonance with one example each.
questions.answer: Free vibrations occur when a body vibrates with its natural frequency after being disturbed, without continuous external force, e.g. a tuning fork struck once. Forced vibrations occur when a body vibrates under a continuous external periodic force, adopting the frequency of that force, e.g. a table vibrating when a vibrating tuning fork is placed on it. Resonance is a special case of forced vibration when the applied frequency equals the natural frequency of the body, producing vibrations of maximum amplitude, e.g. a second identical tuning fork resonating with the first.
questions.explanation: The key difference lies in the source and frequency of vibration.
questions.commonMistake: Clearly state the condition that makes resonance different from ordinary forced vibration.

questions.prompt: Describe how SONAR is used to determine the depth of the sea.
questions.answer: In SONAR, an ultrasonic pulse is transmitted from a ship towards the seabed. The pulse reflects from the seabed and returns as an echo to a receiver on the ship. The time interval between transmission and reception is measured. Since the sound travels down and up, the depth d is calculated using d = vt/2, where v is the speed of sound in seawater and t is the total time taken. This method allows accurate measurement of sea depth and detection of underwater objects.
questions.explanation: Echo timing and known speed of sound in water give the distance.
questions.commonMistake: Use half the total time or divide total distance by 2.

questions.prompt: Explain the characteristics of sound: loudness, pitch and quality, and state the factors on which each depends.
questions.answer: Loudness is the characteristic by which a sound is perceived as loud or soft. It depends mainly on the amplitude of vibration and also on distance from the source and the area of the vibrating surface. Pitch is the characteristic by which a sound is perceived as shrill or flat and depends on the frequency of vibration; higher frequency gives higher pitch. Quality or timbre is the characteristic that distinguishes sounds of the same loudness and pitch produced by different sources, such as a violin and a flute. It depends on the waveform, which is determined by the fundamental and overtones present.
questions.explanation: All three characteristics together describe how sounds are perceived.
questions.commonMistake: Associate each characteristic with the correct physical factor.

questions.prompt: Why are the walls of auditoriums and cinema halls covered with sound-absorbing materials?
questions.answer: In large halls, sound reflects repeatedly from walls, ceiling and other surfaces, causing reverberation. Excessive reverberation makes speech and music unclear because successive sounds overlap. Sound-absorbing materials such as curtains, carpets and acoustic panels reduce reflections and absorb sound energy, thereby decreasing reverberation time and improving clarity of sound for the audience.
questions.explanation: Controlling reflections improves audibility and intelligibility.
questions.commonMistake: Distinguish reverberation from a single echo.

questions.prompt: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 512 Hz are sounded separately. Compare the pitch and state which has the higher pitch. If both produce waves in air at 340 m/s, compare their wavelengths.
questions.answer: Pitch depends on frequency, so the 512 Hz tuning fork produces a sound of higher pitch than the 256 Hz fork. Using v = fλ, wavelength λ = v/f. For 256 Hz, λ = 340/256 ≈ 1.33 m. For 512 Hz, λ = 340/512 ≈ 0.664 m. Thus, the higher-pitch sound has the shorter wavelength.
questions.explanation: At constant speed in the same medium, wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.
questions.commonMistake: Higher frequency means higher pitch and shorter wavelength.

questions.prompt: A ship sends an ultrasonic signal to the seabed and receives the echo after 4 s. If the speed of sound in seawater is 1500 m/s, calculate the depth of the sea. Why is ultrasound preferred over audible sound in such measurements?
questions.answer: Total distance travelled = v × t = 1500 × 4 = 6000 m. Depth of sea = total distance/2 = 6000/2 = 3000 m. Ultrasound is preferred because its high frequency gives shorter wavelengths and better directionality, allowing more accurate detection and ranging. It is also inaudible to humans and less affected by background noise in many applications.
questions.explanation: Echo method gives distance, and ultrasonic waves improve precision and practicality.
questions.commonMistake: Divide by 2 for the one-way depth and state practical reasons for using ultrasound.

questions.prompt: How can resonance be both useful and harmful? Give one example of each.
questions.answer: Resonance is useful when large amplitude vibrations are desired at a specific frequency, such as in musical instruments where air columns resonate to amplify sound. It can be harmful when vibrations become excessively large and damage structures, for example if external periodic forces match the natural frequency of a bridge or building component, causing dangerous oscillations. Therefore, resonance must be controlled depending on the application.
questions.explanation: The same principle of frequency matching can produce beneficial or damaging effects.
questions.commonMistake: Provide clear, relevant examples for both useful and harmful cases.
